cruise_kts.calculation: Airbus gives M0.78 as the A320 family's cruise speed, in an evaluation flown at 35,000 ft (Getting to grips with fuel economy §5.2.2 p. 28). min_runway_ft.calculation: Takeoff weight midway between MLW 62,500 kg and MTOW 75,500 kg (AC 2-1-1 p. 1, WV002) = 69,000 kg = 152,119 lb. AC 3-3-1 p. 2 (take-off weight limitation, ISA, CFM56), sea-level (0) curve at 152,119 lb on the gridded lb axis: ≈5,410 ft of runway (0.71 of the way from the 4,000 ft to the 6,000 ft gridline). Landing at MLW 62,500 kg = 137,789 lb, AC 3-4-1 p. 2 (ISA, slats 27°/flaps 35°, CFM56-5A), sea-level curve: ≈4,640 ft. Longer = takeoff 5,410 ft → up to the next 100 ft = 5,500 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: At the basic weight variant WV000 (MTOW 64,000 kg, MLW 61,000 kg; midpoint 62,500 kg) the same charts give takeoff ≈4,340 ft and landing ≈4,520 ft → 4,600 ft. The IAE V2500 take-off chart (3-3-1 p. 3) at 69,000 kg gives ≈5,400 ft.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude without options. 39,800 ft if modification 30748 is embodied; 41,100 ft with modification 28162 (A319-112/-115/-132/-133 only).

max_xwind_kts.note: The lower of the two demonstrated values: Airbus's A319/A320/A321 FCOM (Operating Limitations), as quoted in the report, gives 'maximum crosswind demonstrated for takeoff: 29 knots gusting up to 38 knots' and 'for landing: 33 knots gusting up to 38 knots'. The report adds (§1.18.5.1, p. 38) that the A320 flight manual records 38 kt (gust included) as the maximum crosswind demonstrated for landing.

climb_fpm.calculation: Getting to grips with the cost index, Table 6 p. 21 (A320, CFM56, 75,000 kg takeoff weight, climb to FL330, ISA, no wind, 250 kt up to FL100), cost index 40: time to climb 23.7 min. 33,000 / 23.7 = 1,392 → 1,400 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: The published climb is to FL330, not to the 35,000 ft cruise altitude; taken as published, not corrected. Cost index 40 is the tabulated value nearest 45, the medium-time/medium-fuel cost index of the guide's Table 2 p. 11 ('A319/A321 cost index', in §3.2 'A320 Family'). Other rows: CI 0 22.4 min (→ 1,450 fpm), CI 100 26.1 min (→ 1,250 fpm).

climb_kts.calculation: Getting to grips with the cost index, Table 6 p. 21 (A320, CFM56, 75,000 kg, climb to FL330, ISA, no wind), cost index 40: 165 nm in 23.7 min. 165 / (23.7 / 60) = 417.7 → 420 kt.
climb_kts.note: Distance and time to FL330, taken as published. CI 0: 150 nm / 22.4 min → 400 kt; CI 100: 187 nm / 26.1 min → 430 kt.

descent_fpm.calculation: Getting to grips with the cost index, Table 15 p. 53 (A320, CFM56, 60,000 kg, descent from FL370, ISA, no wind, 250 kt below FL100), cost index 40: time to descend 14.9 min. 37,000 / 14.9 = 2,483 → 2,500 fpm.
descent_fpm.note: The published descent is from FL370, not from the 35,000 ft cruise altitude, and its end point is not stated; taken as published, not corrected (35,000 / 14.9 would give 2,350 fpm). Cost index 40 as for the climb. CI 0: 19 min (→ 1,950 fpm); CI 80: 14.6 min (→ 2,550 fpm).

entries.variant: Piper PA-24-250 Comanche 250 (2,900 lb gross), Lycoming O-540 (250 hp)

sources.title: Aircraft Specification No. 1A15, Revision 34 (PA-24, PA-24-250, PA-24-260, PA-24-400)
sources.publisher: Federal Aviation Administration (archived copy of the FAA Regulatory and Guidance Library PDF)
sources.page: pp. 2-4, II. Model PA-24-250 (no cabin pressurisation, no maximum operating altitude)

sources.title: The Piper Comanche PA-24-180, PA-24-250 Owner's Handbook, Part No. 753 597, issued November 1961, revised November 1973 (complete scan)
sources.publisher: Piper Aircraft Corporation (scan hosted by the North East Comanche type-club document mirror; identical file at pipercomanche.info)
sources.page: Section I p. 1 (Specification Features: service ceiling); Section III p. 23 (Take-off Performance PA-24-250 table), p. 24 (Climb), p. 25 (Cruising), p. 28 (Landing Performance PA-24-250 table)

pressurised.note: The PA-24-250 section (and the whole specification) gives no cabin pressurisation limits.

cruise_kts.calculation: 'The 250 Comanche has a maximum recommended cruising speed of 181 M.P.H. at 75% power at 7000 feet' (Owner's Handbook p. 25; also p. 1, optimum cruising speed, 75% power, 181 mph): 181 mph / 1.15078 = 157.3 kt -> 157 kt (a published figure converted to knots, kept in whole units)
cruise_kts.note: TAS (the handbook's speeds are true airspeeds, p. 25). At 75% power at sea level the handbook gives 171 mph (p. 1).

min_runway_ft.note: Take-off total distance over 50 ft barrier at 2,900 lb (max gross), sea level, 60°F (the table's row nearest the 59°F standard day), zero wind, 15° Max-Lift flaps (the handbook's only PA-24-250 take-off table; ground run 1,180 ft). Landing over 50 ft barrier at 2,900 lb, sea level, 60°F, zero wind: 1,420 ft (p. 28).

ceiling_ft.note: Manufacturer's service ceiling (1A15 certifies no maximum operating altitude). Absolute ceiling 22,000 ft.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which the handbook quotes the 181 mph cruise (p. 25).

climb_fpm.note: The handbook gives rates of climb (1,350 fpm at sea level, p. 1; rate-of-climb chart p. 42) but no time to climb.

climb_kts.calculation: Climb schedule (p. 24): best rate of climb 105 mph IAS at sea level, decreasing about 1 mph per 1,000 ft, so 98 mph IAS at 7,000 ft. IAS taken as CAS (no position-error data); TAS = CAS / sqrt(sigma), ISA sigma(7,000 ft) = 0.8106. Sea level: 105 mph = 91.2 kt TAS; 7,000 ft: 98 mph = 85.2 kt CAS = 94.6 kt TAS. Average over the climb ≈ (91.2 + 94.6) / 2 = 92.9 kt (a time-weighted average using the p. 42 rate-of-climb line gives 93.0 kt) → 95 kt
climb_kts.note: The handbook also says a good climb is obtained at 100-110 mph at lower altitudes with more forward speed.
